title: Permanent versus determinant
formal: Over the complex numbers, is the sequence \(dc_{C}(\operatorname{perm}_{n})\) unbounded by every polynomial in n? Explicitly, for every \(C>0\) and integer \(k\ge 1\), must there be \(n\ge 1\) such that \(dc_{C}(\operatorname{perm}_{n})>C(n+1)^{k}\)?
definitions: The polynomial perm\(_{n}(X)=\sum_{\sigma \in S_{n}}\prod _{i=1}^{n}x_{i,\sigma (i)}\) has \(n^{2}\) algebraically independent commuting variables and degree \(n; S_{n}\) is the set of permutations of \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). Its determinantal complexity \(dc_{C}(\operatorname{perm}_{n})\) is the smallest positive integer m for which there exist constant complex \(m\times m\) matrices \(A_{0}\) and \(A_{ij}\) satisfying the exact polynomial identity perm\(_{n}(X)=\det (A_{0}+\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}x_{ij}A_{ij})\). Thus every matrix entry is an arbitrary affine-linear form in all input variables. The representation may depend on n and use arbitrary complex constants without a bit-length or constructibility restriction. The resource is matrix dimension m. No symmetry, sparsity, multilinearity of intermediate expressions, regularity, or read-once restriction is imposed. Equality is in \(C[X]\), for every complex substitution, not only on \(0/1\) inputs. Border complexity, which permits a limit of representations, is a separate measure. Characteristic two is excluded by fixing C: in that characteristic the permanent equals the determinant. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
why: A central concrete target in algebraic complexity: determine whether one canonical efficiently computable polynomial can simulate a canonical algebraic counting polynomial at polynomial cost. Its formulation invites tools from algebraic geometry and representation theory while retaining a precise computational meaning.

importance.reason: The principal permanent-versus-determinant lower-bound problem, connecting algebraic computation, branching programs, geometry, and symmetry.

progress.text: Valiant establishes the foundational algebraic simulation framework: formulas and branching programs have small determinantal representations, and the permanent is complete for VNP.
Mignon and Ressayre prove \(dc_{C}(\operatorname{perm}_{n})\ge n^{2}/2\) using Hessian ranks at zeros. This remains a polynomial lower bound.

Grenet gives a \(2^{n}- 1\)-dimensional representation; Landsberg and Ressayre prove exponential optimality when specified symmetries must be respected. Their unrestricted-versus-equivariant comparison is left open.
Kumar and Volk survey the permanent bounds and develop a new singular-locus method for a different explicit polynomial, a diagonal power sum. That theorem does not raise the permanent lower bound.
The algebraic cost of Boolean summation distinguishes permanent and determinant under a local fixed-additive-size simulation requirement, leaving general polynomial-size representations open.
Bogart and Valero’s journal paper studies generalized permanents and continues to state the superpolynomial ordinary-permanent problem as open.

status_note: Open in the cited foundational and recent papers; checked through 10 September 2026. This card fixes exact unrestricted representations over C. Symmetric, equivariant, real-field, border, and other-polynomial bounds are not substituted for this model.

context_blocks.text: The permanent and determinant sum the same products indexed by permutations; the determinant attaches a permutation sign. Those signs enable cancellations behind efficient determinant computation. A determinantal representation asks whether a larger matrix with carefully chosen affine entries can reproduce the unsigned sum exactly. Merely showing that changing signs in the original \(n\times n\) matrix fails leaves almost all permitted representations untouched.

The model is nonuniform and algebraic. It asks about the existence of a family of polynomial-size representations even if finding their complex coefficients is computationally difficult. Determinants characterize polynomial-size algebraic branching programs up to polynomial overhead, whereas unrestricted arithmetic circuits define the potentially larger class VP. The requested lower bound separates the permanent from the branching-program model; it should not be identified without qualification with a separation from all of VP.

The unrestricted complex-field lower bound is still quadratic in the original matrix dimension: Mignon and Ressayre prove \(dc_{C}(\operatorname{perm}_{n})\ge n^{2}/2\). Their argument compares the rank of the matrix of second partial derivatives, the Hessian, at carefully chosen zeros of the two polynomials. Because the permanent has \(n^{2}\) input variables, this is only linear in its number of variables, despite being quadratic in n.

There is also an explicit exponential upper bound, \(dc_{C}(\operatorname{perm}_{n})\le 2^{n}- 1\), due to Grenet. Landsberg and Ressayre prove that this construction is optimal under particular equivariance requirements involving permutations and diagonal rescaling. Removing those requirements is essential: the question allows a representation to break every visible symmetry of the polynomial. Whether symmetry can be imposed with only polynomial overhead is itself another open problem.

Progress can reveal structural differences without giving an unrestricted lower bound. Orzel, Srinivasan, Tavenas, and Yehudayoff show that a local Boolean-summation operation can be absorbed into a permanent by a fixed additive increase in dimension, whereas the analogous uniform fixed-additive-cost property fails for determinants. Their FSTTCS 2025 result explains a step in the VNP-completeness construction; it does not exclude a different, global polynomial-size determinant representation.

Bogart and Valero extend upper- and lower-bound techniques to two generalized permanent families. Their 2026 journal version still identifies the Mignon–Ressayre estimate as the best known characteristic-zero bound for the ordinary permanent for \(n\ge 5\). This provides a recent status check while illustrating how sensitive the geometric lower-bound method is to the polynomial being studied.

sentences: The permanent adds permutation products without the signs that occur in a determinant.
This problem asks whether representing it as the determinant of a larger matrix of affine linear forms requires superpolynomial dimension.
The representation may use arbitrary complex constants and break all symmetries of the original polynomial.
Such a lower bound would separate permanent computation from determinant-like branching programs, rather than automatically from every arithmetic circuit.
The saved review places quadratic unrestricted lower bounds beside exponential constructions, leaving a large gap that symmetry-restricted results cannot close.
